content:
At a rally in Texas for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, President Donald Trump had his speech interrupted multiple times by over a dozen protesters, whom he then berated from the stage.

"That guy's gotta lose some weight," Trump said as the protester was being removed.

Referring to another protester, he said: "He's going home to find his mommy... but what he doesn't know is his mommy voted for Trump."

The president also baselessly claimed the protesters were paid to heckle. "These are paid protesters, paid by enemies of our country," Trump said without any evidence.

His body language and facial expressions betrayed a lot as he spoke and watched the protesters move through the crowd.

Denise Dudley, a clinical psychologist and behavioral expert, said: "One thing to remember about this scene is that he's on his home turf. This is not a bipartisan thing... he's with his people. So he doesn't just have the protesters removed, he uses them."

Dudley added that he employed a technique called "reframing for the audience," "meaning he took the protester's disruption and turned it into an opportunity to more clearly define the event for his supporters."

She said Trump created an "in-group/out-group" dynamic — a way people distinguish supporters from critics, even "good people" from "bad people."

Trump repeatedly commented on the motives and appearance of those who opposed him.

Dudley said: "He's describing the out-group to the in-group, and that excites the in-group more... they start chanting 'USA,' so he uses this very effectively, saying essentially: 'Look at us, then look at those scary people over there. They're paid protesters.'"

She added: "He's essentially attacking them to, in a sense, pull his own side closer together. So it's a tactic."

Experts pointed out that Trump made tongue movements at certain moments, which indicated irritation.

Patti Wood, a body language expert and author of *Snap: Making the Most of First Impressions, Body Language, and Charisma*, said that throughout the rally, Trump made repeated tongue movements, which spoke volumes.

At one point, "he was pressing his tongue against the inside of his cheek and pushing outward — that's an irritation gesture."

Wood said: "He also did what's called a 'tongue jut' when irritated, which is sticking the tongue out."

She said: "This is one of my favorite nonverbal behaviors to see on people in power, because it's like the big kids on the playground who, when they're bullying a kid who can't fight back, stick their tongue out like that."

She noted that this gesture was brief but a "very primal" response.

Wood said: "This is an indicator of his irritation, and he does it before he launches an attack."

Wood said: "I see this a lot in prisoner escorts... not on presidents in any context, because they hold the power. So this tells me that, on some level, he doesn't feel he holds the power, and that's quite a revealing thing."

His clenched jaw and tight-pressed lips showed he was tense and trying to restrain himself.

Behavioral scientist Abbie Maroño said: "When you look at his face, you can't help but notice his lips."

Trump frequently made many mouth and lip movements as he spoke and interacted.

Maroño said Trump "does press his lips when irritated very often. So his baseline is already a lot of lip movement, but this was particularly exaggerated."

She said it's interesting that this happened every time he tried to positively reframe the protesters' disruption.

Maroño said: "He had very extreme lip compression. And lip compression is a behavior we use to almost hide information... it's a restraining gesture, something we do when we're trying to restrain ourselves, feeling displeased or embarrassed and want to say something."

Wood added that lip compression can have multiple meanings, but it generally signals disgust.

Maroño noted that his jaw was also visibly clenched. "You can see how tense and prominent it is... it's not just clenched, it's moving forward constantly."

Maroño said this signaled an "extreme" level of abnormality, and he was trying to suppress irritation and frustration.

Experts said when protesters were being removed, he would stop and stare at them — a "selfish move."

As some protesters were being escorted out, Trump deliberately paused his speech to stare at them being removed. This also made everyone else pause and watch.

Dudley said: "Whether you're in the audience or watching the rally on TV, it's 'nothing is happening until those protesters are removed.'"

Dudley said: "He just stops and stares — that forces all of us to know the protesters are being removed. Even if we can't see them, we all know." In a sense, this was making an example of the protesters.

Dudley said: "I think this is, in some ways, the most selfish move you could make." She added that people came to the rally to hear Trump speak, but he stopped the entire event to stare and wait.

She said this was his way of bringing the whole rally to a halt and making everyone watch the "naughty protesters" being taken away.

Certain head movements and mouth expressions showed Trump felt "irritated" and "fatigued" by the disruptions.

Maroño said: "I noticed that several times he would lift his chin, and we typically do that when we feel proud or are trying to project confidence."

She noted that this is why people remind themselves to hold their head up when trying to appear confident.

She said: "He kept lifting his chin several times, so he's trying to project confidence." But combined with his hidden irritation, Maroño added, this created a vibe of "combative confidence."

She said: "He's not calm and composed. He's composed, but with irritation."

With over 12 disruptions throughout the night, it's no wonder Trump felt irritated — even if he didn't want the protesters to know they were getting to him.

Maroño said: "Now it's so close to the election, it's like a war that's gone on and on, you were full of drive and fighting spirit, but by the end, like at the final sprint when you're so close, you become utterly exhausted."

She added: "I'm starting to see a bit more of this in his recent appearances, he's starting to look a bit irritated."

Wood agreed, noting that after Trump's "these are paid protesters" remark, his eyes would "flicker," and his mouth would have a downturned arc.

Wood said: "This tells me... he feels fatigued. His delivery lacks power, and then he feels fatigued at the thought of them even being there."

Trump's supporters also booed the protesters, which Wood said she thought confused Trump.

Wood said: "For a moment I was even wondering, was he thinking: 'Are those boos for me?' Like what happened to him at a football game." Trump was booed last year at a Washington Commanders game.

Wood said: "I think this shows the negative rhetoric from these people got to him."

Wood added that his pausing before responding or acknowledging the situation also showed he had to first figure out what he actually wanted to do or say.

His instinct was to attack immediately, ignore people, or cut them off, but "he didn't do that this time."

Wood said: "In that immediate attacking, he's not his usual self."
